title: Small Pushes, Large Effects
paragraphs: Public discussion of climate change tends to fix on carbon dioxide, and for good reason: the gas is the main lever that human activity has pulled. Yet the mechanism by which it warms the planet involves more than the gas itself, and the fuller picture helps explain why small changes matter. That is why the subject rewards patient explanation far more than confident slogans.

The basic physics is a natural greenhouse effect: certain gases absorb heat and slow its escape into space, keeping the surface warm enough for life. Carbon dioxide comes from natural sources such as volcanoes and from human activities such as burning fossil fuels and clearing forests. NASA reports that its concentration in the atmosphere has risen by nearly fifty percent since seventeen fifty.

Water vapour complicates the account. It is the most abundant greenhouse gas, yet it is not a direct cause of warming: it responds to temperature, because warmer oceans put more of it into the air, and the extra vapour then amplifies the original warming. The result is a feedback: a modest initial push from carbon dioxide is magnified by the system it disturbs.

Evidence for how the system behaves comes partly from ice cores. Drilled in Greenland, Antarctica and tropical glaciers, they contain tiny bubbles of ancient air whose composition can be compared with recent direct measurements. They show that Earth's climate has always responded to changes in greenhouse gases.

What is new is the pace. NASA states that carbon dioxide added by people is increasing roughly two hundred and fifty times faster than it did from natural sources after the last ice age. A system that amplifies small pushes is least forgiving when the push is large and sudden. Understanding that logic does not prescribe a policy, but it explains why the timing of any policy matters.

sources.claim: Sera etkisi doğaldır: bazı gazlar ısıyı emip uzaya kaçışını yavaşlatır; karbondioksit volkanlar gibi doğal kaynaklardan ve fosil yakıt yakma ile ormansızlaşmadan gelir; atmosferdeki karbondioksit 1750'den beri yaklaşık yüzde 50 arttı.
